680.title: The Nativity of Mary (8 September)
680.hook: nine months after the Immaculate Conception, a birthday for Mary
680.tomorrow: The Exaltation of the Cross (14 September)
680.howItsDone: Catholics keep the feast of the Nativity of the Blessed Virgin Mary on 8 September, nine months after the Immaculate Conception; the Gospel is Matthew's genealogy, and in places such as Malta and parts of Italy and India the day is marked with processions and festivals.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Assumption, Mary taken up. Your line was she went ahead. Whom did you picture on the road ahead of you? Day six hundred eighty.

Count back nine months from the eighth of September, and you land on the eighth of December. That's the Immaculate Conception, the feast of Mary's conception in her mother's womb. The Church's calendar does the arithmetic on purpose. So today is a birthday. In Malta it's a public holiday; in Italian towns and in parts of India there are processions and sweets. And the Gospel the Church reads for it is one that's easy to skip: the long list of names at the start of Matthew.
screen: `DECEMBER TO SEPTEMBER: NINE MONTHS.` → `A BIRTHDAY.` → `A LIST OF NAMES.`

segments.voice: Like her parents' names, Mary's birth isn't told in the Bible. The details again come from the Protoevangelium of James, and an old tradition places her birth in Jerusalem, near the pool of Bethesda, where a church of Saint Anne stands today. The feast began in the East, and Rome took it up later. So why read a genealogy on her birthday? Matthew counts it out as three sets of fourteen generations, from Abraham through David and the exile, and it's not all heroes. It includes a man who helped sell his brother, a king who arranged a soldier's death, and women with complicated stories, Tamar, Rahab, Ruth, and the wife of Urias. Generation after generation of ordinary, mixed-up people. And then the list breaks its own pattern. Line after line, it's been so-and-so begot so-and-so. At the end, in the Douay-Rheims: "And Jacob begot Joseph the husband of Mary, of whom was born Jesus, who is called Christ." The rhythm stops at her. Mary's birthday is the Church saying: here is the place where the long, crooked family line was heading. One ordinary-looking girl, born, tradition says, to an older couple, in a city full of pilgrims. Catholics greet her today, often with the angel's own words from Luke: "Hail, full of grace, the Lord is with thee: blessed art thou among women." There's no cake in the liturgy. But in some towns, there is cake.
screen: `NOT IN THE BIBLE; A TRADITION.` · `THREE SETS OF FOURTEEN.` · `NOT ALL HEROES.` · `THE RHYTHM STOPS AT HER.` · then, large: `OF WHOM WAS BORN JESUS, WHO IS CALLED CHRIST.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: wish Mary a happy birthday. It's a simple, almost childlike thing, and that's the point. Sit, and think about the people who were part of the line that led to you: names you know, names you don't. Then, if you pray, greet Mary the way Catholics do, with the angel's words, Hail, full of grace, and wish her a happy birthday. If you don't pray, think of a birthday you've forgotten lately, and plan to honor it. The bell holds the time.
Nativitas Mariae. Latin for the birth of Mary, kept nine months after the Immaculate Conception, on the eighth of September. Today's word.
Your line: her birthday. Today, find out one name from your own family line that you didn't know, a great-grandparent or further back. Day six hundred eighty.

681.title: The Exaltation of the Cross (14 September)
681.hook: the cross found in Jerusalem, honored as a tree of life
681.howItsDone: Catholics celebrate the feast of the Exaltation of the Holy Cross on 14 September with red vestments and the Gloria; the Gospel is John 3:13–17, and some parishes hold a veneration of a relic or crucifix.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Nativity of Mary, Nativitas Mariae, and a long list of names. Your line was her birthday. Which name from your own family line did you find? Day six hundred eighty-one.

The Bible begins in a garden with a tree in the middle of it, the tree of life, and ends in a city where the tree of life grows again, beside a river. In between, Christians say, there's a third tree: two beams of rough wood on a hill outside Jerusalem. Good Friday is the day the Church grieves at that tree. But there's a second day for the cross, in September, with no grief in it at all. The priest wears red, the Gloria is sung, and the Church calls the cross by a startling name.
screen: `A TREE IN THE GARDEN.` → `A TREE IN THE CITY.` → `A THIRD TREE ON A HILL.`

segments.voice: The feast's story begins with Helena, the mother of the emperor Constantine. Tradition says that late in her life she traveled to Jerusalem and had the hill of Calvary excavated, and that the wood of the cross was found there. Historians can't confirm the details, and the Church tells it as tradition. Constantine built a great church over the site of the tomb and Calvary. Tradition keeps its dedication on the thirteenth of September, and on the next day, the fourteenth, the cross was lifted up and shown to the people. That's what exaltation means: lifting high. Centuries later, the story goes, the relic was carried off by a Persian army and brought back by the emperor Heraclius, and that homecoming became part of the feast too. The Gospel for the day is John three, where Jesus compares himself to the bronze serpent Moses raised in the desert, which healed anyone who looked at it. In the Douay-Rheims: "as Moses lifted up the serpent in the desert, so must the Son of man be lifted up." The thing that should mean death is lifted up as healing. Old Latin hymns sing this. One line by the poet Venantius Fortunatus, still sung on Good Friday, begins "Crux fidelis, inter omnes arbor una nobilis": faithful cross, the one noble tree among all trees. In the hymn, the instrument of execution becomes the tree of life. Today's feast is about that reversal.
screen: `HELENA IN JERUSALEM.` · `A CHURCH OVER CALVARY; LIFTED HIGH.` · `THE BRONZE SERPENT.` · `THE ONE NOBLE TREE.` · then, large: `SO MUST THE SON OF MAN BE LIFTED UP.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: a slow sign of the cross. Sit, and breathe. Then trace the cross on yourself as slowly as you can, as if your hand were lifting something heavy and good. Forehead. Chest. Left shoulder. Right shoulder. Stay with it. Then think of one thing in your life that once felt like a dead end and became a way through. If you don't make the sign, simply trace a cross in the air or on the table with one finger, slowly. The bell holds the time.
Crux fidelis. Latin for faithful cross, the line Venantius Fortunatus wrote calling it the one noble tree among all trees. Today's word.
Your line: the tree of life. Today, look at one real tree on your way, and think of the thing that turned from a dead end into a way through. Day six hundred eighty-one.

682.title: Our Lady of Sorrows (15 September)
682.hook: the day after the cross, his mother
682.howItsDone: Catholics keep the memorial of Our Lady of Sorrows on 15 September, the day after the Exaltation of the Cross; the Stabat Mater may be sung as an optional sequence, and some pray the chaplet of the Seven Sorrows.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Exaltation of the Cross, Crux fidelis, lifted high. Your line was the tree of life. What turned from a dead end into a way through? Day six hundred eighty-two.

Anyone who has sat beside a hospital bed knows the feeling of being unable to do anything. You can't fix it. You can't take the pain. All you can do is not leave. Yesterday the Church lifted the cross high. Today, the very next day, it turns to look at the person standing at the foot of it. Not the soldiers, not the crowd. His mother. The feast is Our Lady of Sorrows, and its word is the opening of a medieval poem.
screen: `BESIDE A HOSPITAL BED.` → `YESTERDAY THE CROSS.` → `TODAY, HIS MOTHER.`

segments.voice: John's Gospel gives the scene in one line, in the Douay-Rheims: "Now there stood by the cross of Jesus, his mother." She stood. The other Gospels say many watched from a distance. John puts her close enough to hear him speak, and from the cross Jesus gives her to the beloved disciple, and the disciple to her. In the 1200s someone wrote a Latin poem on that one verb. It begins: "Stabat Mater dolorosa, juxta crucem lacrimosa." The sorrowful mother stood, weeping, beside the cross. It's often credited to the Franciscan poet Jacopone da Todi, though nobody can be sure. Today it may be sung at Mass as a sequence, and it's sung in many churches between the Stations of the Cross. Composers from Palestrina to Pergolesi to Dvořák set it to music. The feast also gathers up seven sorrows that Catholic devotion counts in Mary's life: Simeon's warning in the Temple that a sword would pierce her soul; the flight into Egypt; losing the twelve-year-old Jesus for three days; meeting him on the way to the cross; standing at the cross; receiving his body; and the burial. Simeon's line is in Luke: "And thy own soul a sword shall pierce." In paintings, she's shown with seven swords in her heart. What the feast honors isn't a mother who understood everything or could change anything. It's a mother who stayed.
screen: `SHE STOOD BY THE CROSS.` · `STABAT MATER DOLOROSA.` · `SEVEN SORROWS.` · `A MOTHER WHO STAYED.` · then, large: `NOW THERE STOOD BY THE CROSS OF JESUS, HIS MOTHER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: hold a grieving mother. Sit, and think of a mother who is grieving: a child lost, a child sick, a child far away or estranged, a child in prison. Maybe someone you know; maybe a face from the news. Picture her, standing where she has to stand. Don't try to fix anything. If you pray, you can pray for her, or pray a Hail Mary for her. If you don't, simply stay with her in your mind. The bell holds the time.
Stabat Mater. Latin for the mother stood: the opening of the medieval poem about Mary at the cross, sung on Our Lady of Sorrows. Today's word.
Your line: the mother stood. Today, if someone near you is going through something you can't fix, don't fix it. Just stay a little longer than is comfortable. Day six hundred eighty-two.

683.title: Saint Francis (4 October)
683.hook: the day animals are brought to church for blessing
683.tomorrow: Our Lady of the Rosary (7 October)
683.howItsDone: Catholics keep the memorial of Saint Francis of Assisi on 4 October, and many parishes hold a blessing of animals on or near the day; Franciscans celebrate it as a solemnity.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Our Lady of Sorrows and the poem Stabat Mater. Your line was the mother stood. Who did you stay with a little longer? Day six hundred eighty-three.

On or near the fourth of October, parish parking lots fill up with dogs on leashes, cats in carriers, a hamster in a shoebox, sometimes a horse, a goat, a goldfish in a bowl, and once in a while a very patient iguana. A priest walks down the line with holy water and blesses each one. It's noisy and a little chaotic, and people who haven't been to church in years show up. The man behind it all died centuries ago, and near the end of his life, nearly blind and in pain, he wrote a song.
screen: `DOGS, CATS, A GOLDFISH.` → `A BLESSING FOR EACH ONE.` → `A SONG FROM A SICKBED.`

segments.voice: Francis of Assisi was the son of a rich cloth merchant. He wanted to be a knight. Instead, after illness and a stint as a prisoner of war, he gave it all up, stripping off even his clothes before the bishop and his father, and lived in poverty, rebuilding ruined churches, caring for lepers, preaching peace. Others came to share that life, and then more. The stories about animals are famous: preaching to the birds, making peace with a wolf that terrified the town of Gubbio. Those come from collections written after his death, and people tell them as stories. But the song is his own. Near the end of his life, sick and almost blind, staying at San Damiano, he wrote the Canticle of the Creatures, not in Latin but in the everyday Italian of Umbria. It begins Laudato si', mi' Signore, praised be you, my Lord, and then it praises God through creation, calling each part family: brother sun, who brings the day; sister moon and the stars; brother wind; sister water, useful and humble and precious and pure; brother fire; and our sister, mother earth. Near his death he added one more verse, for sister death. The idea is older than Francis. The Book of Daniel, in the Catholic Bible, has three young men in a furnace singing, in the Douay-Rheims: "All ye works of the Lord, bless the Lord." What Francis added was the family. Not resources. Not scenery. Kin. In 2015 a pope who took his name borrowed the first line for a letter on care for the earth.
screen: `A RICH MAN'S SON GIVES IT ALL UP.` · `BIRDS AND A WOLF: STORIES TOLD.` · `THE CANTICLE OF THE CREATURES.` · `BROTHER SUN, SISTER WATER.` · then, large: `ALL YE WORKS OF THE LORD, BLESS THE LORD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: bless an animal. If you have a pet, sit beside it and rest a hand on it. If you don't, find an animal you can see: a bird at the window, a dog across the street, even an ant on the sidewalk, or picture one you've loved. Watch it breathe. Notice that it's alive, the way you are. If you pray, you can ask God to bless it. If you don't, wish it well, as kin. The bell holds the time.
Saint Francis. Francis of Assisi, the poor man who called the sun his brother and the earth his sister. His feast is the fourth of October. Today's word.
Your line: brother sun. Today, when you step into sunlight, greet it the way Francis did, as family, even silently. Day six hundred eighty-three.

684.title: Our Lady of the Rosary (7 October)
684.hook: October is the month of the rosary
684.howItsDone: Catholics keep the memorial of Our Lady of the Rosary on 7 October and dedicate October to the rosary; many pray it daily that month, alone, as families, or in parish groups, meditating on the joyful, sorrowful, glorious and luminous mysteries.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Saint Francis and his song of the creatures. Your line was brother sun. Did you greet it? Day six hundred eighty-four.

Look at the rearview mirror of a taxi in Manila or Mexico City, or in the coat pocket of an old man on a bus in Kraków, and there's a decent chance you'll find a string of beads with a small cross at the end. Some people pray on it every day. Some carry it and haven't prayed it in years. Some were handed one at a funeral and kept it in a drawer. On the seventh of October the Church keeps a feast in its name, and the whole month belongs to it.
screen: `BEADS ON A REARVIEW MIRROR.` → `IN A POCKET, IN A DRAWER.` → `A FEAST, AND A MONTH.`

segments.voice: The word rosary comes from the Latin rosarium, a rose garden. In the Middle Ages, a garland of prayers was pictured as a crown of roses offered to Mary. The shape grew out of the psalms. Monks prayed all hundred and fifty psalms; lay people who couldn't read began praying a hundred and fifty Hail Marys or Our Fathers instead, counted on beads or knots. It was sometimes called Mary's psalter. A popular story says Mary gave the rosary to Saint Dominic. Historians find the rosary taking shape gradually over the centuries instead, and the Dominicans did a great deal to spread it. Then the feast. On the seventh of October, 1571, the fleet of the Holy League, an alliance Pope Pius V had helped build, met the Ottoman navy at Lepanto, off the coast of Greece. Pius had asked Christians to pray the rosary. When word came of the victory, he set up a feast of Our Lady of Victory; his successor renamed it Our Lady of the Rosary. In the 1880s Pope Leo XIII wrote letter after letter about the rosary and gave it the whole month of October. The prayer itself is simple: five decades, each an Our Father, ten Hail Marys and a Glory Be, while you think through a mystery from the lives of Jesus and Mary. Joyful, sorrowful, glorious, and in 2002 John Paul II added the luminous mysteries, from Jesus's public life. The beads keep count so the mind can go somewhere else: to Bethlehem, to the garden, to the empty tomb.
screen: `ROSARIUM: A ROSE GARDEN.` · `150 HAIL MARYS FOR 150 PSALMS.` · `LEPANTO, 7 OCTOBER 1571.` · `FIVE DECADES, FOUR SETS OF MYSTERIES.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: plan five decades this week. Today, pray one, or just begin. If you have beads, hold them. If not, use your ten fingers. Choose one scene to think about: a birth in a stable, perhaps, or the empty tomb. If you pray, pray an Our Father and as many Hail Marys as the bell allows, keeping the scene in mind. If you don't, simply move from finger to finger, one breath each, picturing the scene. Then pick four more days this week. The bell holds the time.
rosarium. Latin for a rose garden, the garland of psalms and Hail Marys that grew into the rosary. Today's word.
Your line: the month of beads. Today, put a rosary, or any string of beads, somewhere you'll see it, in a pocket, by the bed, on the mirror. Day six hundred eighty-four.

685.title: All Saints (1 November)
685.howItsDone: Catholics celebrate All Saints on 1 November as a solemnity and, in many countries, a holy day of obligation, with the Beatitudes as the Gospel; in some parishes children dress as saints the evening before.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Our Lady of the Rosary, rosarium, and a garden of prayers. Your line was the month of beads. Where did you put them? Day six hundred eighty-five.

The Church's calendar is crowded with saints: apostles and martyrs, popes and peasants, page after page of names, each with a day. And yet, behind those names, the Church believes there's a crowd beyond counting. A farmer in a village nobody's heard of who prayed every morning of his life. A night nurse. A man who quietly forgave his brother. No statue, no day, no feast. So once a year the Church throws them all one party. Today, All Saints.
screen: `PAGE AFTER PAGE OF NAMES.` → `A CROWD BEYOND COUNTING.` → `ONE FEAST FOR ALL OF THEM.`

segments.voice: The feast grew from the martyrs. In the early centuries there were so many that no calendar could hold them, and Christians in the East began keeping one day for all martyrs together. In Rome, Pope Boniface IV took the Pantheon, the old temple to all the Roman gods, and dedicated it to Mary and all the martyrs. Later, Pope Gregory III dedicated a chapel at Saint Peter's to all the saints, and the first of November became the date, spreading across the West. The reading for the day comes from Revelation, in the Douay-Rheims: "After this I saw a great multitude, which no man could number, of all nations, and tribes, and peoples, and tongues, standing before the throne." Which no man could number. That's the point. A saint, in Catholic teaching, isn't only someone the Church has formally canonized. Canonization says, with confidence, this person is in heaven, and can be held up as an example. But everyone in heaven is a saint, and the Church assumes that's a huge crowd, most of them never named. The Gospel for the day is the Beatitudes: blessed are the poor in spirit, the meek, the merciful, the peacemakers. Not a list of famous deeds. A description of ordinary people living a certain way. In the Catholic calendar, All Saints is a solemnity and, in many countries, a holy day of obligation. And it opens a two-day pair: tomorrow, all who have died.
screen: `FIRST, ALL THE MARTYRS.` · `THE PANTHEON, FOR THE MARTYRS.` · `A MULTITUDE NO ONE COULD NUMBER.` · `MOST OF THEM NEVER NAMED.` · then, large: `A GREAT MULTITUDE, WHICH NO MAN COULD NUMBER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: think of an unknown holy person. Sit, and let someone come to mind whose goodness nobody ever wrote down. A relative, a teacher, the woman who ran the parish soup kitchen, a neighbor who checked on everyone. Living or dead. Picture their hands and what those hands did. If you pray, you can thank God for them, or ask their prayers, as Catholics do. If you don't, simply honor them, silently, for the length of the bell. The bell holds the time.
All Saints. The first of November, a feast for every saint in heaven, the known and the unknown, the multitude no one could number. Today's word.
Your line: the ones nobody knew. Today, tell one person about the holy person you thought of, so that at least one more person knows. Day six hundred eighty-five.

686.title: All Souls (2 November)
686.hook: November is the month of the dead; graves visited and names read
686.tomorrow: The Dedication of the Lateran (9 November)
686.howItsDone: On All Souls Day, 2 November, Catholics pray for the dead, attend Mass, and visit and decorate graves; through November many parishes keep a book of names of the dead near the altar and read aloud the names of parishioners who died that year.

segments.voice: Yesterday, All Saints, the multitude no one could number. Your line was the ones nobody knew. Whom did you tell about yours? Day six hundred eighty-six.

In the first days of November, the cemeteries of Poland glow after dark. Small candles in red and white glass jars flicker on grave after grave, the famous and the forgotten, until a whole hillside looks like a field of embers. In Mexico, families sit at graves with marigolds and food. In a parish church in Ohio, a priest stands at the ambo and reads aloud, one by one, the names of everyone from the parish who died in the past year. Today, All Souls.
screen: `CANDLES ON EVERY GRAVE.` → `MARIGOLDS AND FOOD.` → `THE NAMES READ ALOUD.`

segments.voice: Yesterday was for all the saints in heaven. Today is for all the faithful departed: everyone who has died, and especially those who, Catholics believe, are still being made ready for God. The Church calls that purification purgatory. It isn't a second chance or a halfway hell. It's understood as the last stretch of being healed, and Catholics believe the living can help with their prayers. One scripture the Church points to is in the second book of Maccabees, which is in the Catholic Bible. After a battle, Judas Maccabeus takes up a collection so that sacrifice can be offered for the fallen, and the text says, in the Douay-Rheims: "It is therefore a holy and wholesome thought to pray for the dead." Christians differ here. Catholics and Orthodox Christians pray for the dead; many Protestant churches do not, and Protestant Bibles leave Maccabees out or set it apart with the Apocrypha. As a single day, All Souls comes from a monastery. Odilo, an abbot of the great monastery of Cluny in France, ordered his monks to pray for all the dead on the day after All Saints, and the custom spread. During the First World War, with so many dying, Pope Benedict XV allowed every priest to celebrate three Masses on this day. The old Latin prayer for the dead, still said at funerals and graves, is short: "Requiem aeternam dona eis, Domine." Eternal rest give unto them, O Lord. That's where the word requiem comes from. And week ninety-eight closes: Mary's birthday, the cross lifted high, the mother who stood, Francis, the rosary, all the saints, and now all the dead.

segments.voice: Here's the practice: visit or remember a grave. If there's a cemetery near you, and you have time today or this week, go, and stand at a grave you know. If not, sit, and bring one person who has died to mind. Say their full name, out loud if you can. Remember one specific thing: a voice, a phrase, a smell. If you pray, you can say the old line, eternal rest give unto them, O Lord. If you don't, simply remember. The bell holds the time.
All Souls. The second of November, when Catholics pray for all the faithful departed, and the beginning of the month of the dead. Today's word.
Your line: we remember. Today, write down the names of people you've lost, and keep the list somewhere you'll see it this month. Day six hundred eighty-six.
